entries.25cef0205dc4113341dcd0e502f15239d84f154c:
Verse 36. But now. The Saviour says the times are changed. Before, he sent them out only for a little time. They were in their own country. Their journeys would be short, and there was no need that they should make preparation for a long absence, or for encountering great dangers. But now they were to go into the wide world, among strangers, trials, dangers, and wants. And as the time was near; as he was about to die; as these dangers pressed on, it was proper that they should make provision for what was before them.

A purse. Mt 10:9. He intimates that they should now take money, as it would be necessary to provide for their wants in travelling.

Scrip. Mt 10:10.

And he that hath no sword. There has been much difficulty in understanding why Jesus directed his disciples to arm themselves, as if it was his purpose to make a defence. It is certain that the spirit of his religion is against the use of the sword, and that it was not his purpose to defend himself against Judas. But it should be remembered that these directions about the purse, the scrip, and the sword were not made with reference to his being taken in the garden, but with reference to their future life. The time of the trial in Gethsemane was just at hand; nor was there time then, if no other reason existed, to go and make the purchase. It altogether refers to their future life. They were going into the midst of dangers. The country was infested with robbers and wild beasts. It was customary to go armed. He tells them of those dangers-of the necessity of being prepared in the usual way to meet them. This, then, is not to be considered as a specific, positive command to procure a sword, but an intimation that great dangers were before them; that their manner of life would be changed, and that they would need the provisions appropriate to that kind of life. The common preparation for that manner of life consisted in money, provisions, and arms; and he foretells them of that manner of life by giving them directions commonly understood to be appropriate to it. It amounts, then, to a prediction that they would soon leave the places which they had been accustomed to, and go into scenes of poverty, want, and danger, where they would feel the necessity of money, provisions, and the means of defence. All, therefore, that the passage justifies is--

1st. That it is proper for men to provide beforehand for their wants, and for ministers and missionaries as well as any others.

2nd. That self-defence is lawful. Men encompassed with danger may lawfully defend their lives. It does not prove that it is lawful to make offensive war on a nation or an individual.

Let him, sell his garment. His mantle or his outer garment. Mt 5:40. The meaning is, let him procure one at any expense, even if he is obliged to sell his clothes for it--intimating that the danger would be very great and pressing.
entries.5268838cdf25e138cf2853d7d11db84b79e146b4:
Verse 37. This that is written. Is 53:12.

Was reckoned among the transgressors. Not reckoned as a transgressor, but among or with them--that is, he was treated as transgressors are. He was put to death in their company, and as he would have been if he had been a transgressor. He was innocent, holy, harmless, and undefiled, He 7:26. God knew this always, and could not think of him, or make him to be otherwise than he was; yet it pleased him to bruise him, and to give him into the hands of men who did reckon him as a transgressor, and who treated him accordingly.

Have an end. This may either mean, "shall be surely accomplished," or "they are about to be fulfilled," or "are now fulfilled." The former is probably the meaning, denoting that every prophecy in regard to him would certainly be accomplished.

(y) "reckoned with transgressors" Is 53:12
entries.f87ab52f0f678af3ba45f06977912f744fbcecc2:
Verse 38. Are two swords. The Galileans, it is said, often went armed. The Essenes did so also. The reason was that the country was full of robbers and wild beasts, and it was necessary to carry, in their travels, some means of defence. It seems that the disciples followed the customs of the country, and had with them them some means of defence, though they had but two swords among the twelve.

It is enough. It is difficult to understand this. Some suppose that it is spoken ironically; as if he had said, "You are bravely armed indeed, with two swords among twelve men, and to meet such a host!" Others, that he meant to reprove them for understanding him literally, as if he meant that they were then to procure swords for immediate battle. As if he had said, "This is absurd, or a perversion of my meaning. I did not intend this, but merely to foretell you of impending dangers after my death." It is to be observed that he did not say "the two swords are enough," but "it is enough;" perhaps meaning simply, enough has been said. Other matters press on, and you will yet understand what I mean.

Verse 43. Strengthening him. His human nature, to sustain the great burden that was upon his soul. Some have supposed from this that he was not divine as well as human; for if he was God, how could an angel give any strength or comfort? and why did not the divine nature alone sustain the human? But the fact that he was divine does not affect the case at all. It might be asked with the same propriety, If he was, as all admit, the friend of God, and beloved of God, and holy, why, if he was a mere man, did not God sustain him alone, without an angel's intervening ? But the objection in neither case would have any force. The man, Christ Jesus, was suffering. His human nature was in agony, and it is the manner of God to sustain the afflicted by the intervention of others; nor was there any more unfitness in sustaining the human nature of his Son in this manner than any other sufferer.

entries.9fd956ce35627fd6cffc91374bba34424a7cc6d1: Verse 48. Betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss? By the Son of man was evidently meant the Messiah. Judas had had the most satisfactory evidence of that, and did not doubt it. A kiss was the sign of affection. By that slight artifice Judas thought to conceal his base purpose. Jesus with severity reproaches him for it. Every word is emphatic. Betrayest thou--dost thou violate all thy obligations of fidelity, and deliver thy Master up to death? Betrayest thou-- thou, so long with him, so much favoured, so sure that this is the Messiah? Betrayest thou the Son of man--the Messiah, the hope of the nations, the desire of all people, the world's Redeemer? Betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss--the sign of friendship and affection employed in a base and wicked purpose, intending to add deceit, disguise, and the prostitution of a mark of affection to the crime of treason? Every word of this must have gone to the very soul of Judas. Perhaps few reproofs of crime more resemble the awful searchings of the souls of the wicked in the day of judgment.

entries.06a53a257d9043fc16baf392cc1401f908fcb449: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.17" sID="gen102429" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102430" type="x-p"/>As Luke mentions that <hi type="italic">the cup </hi>was twice presented by Christ, we must inquire, in the first place, if it be a repetition, (as the Evangelists are wont frequently to say the same thing twice,) or if Christ, after having tasted the cup, repeated the same thing a second time. This latter conjecture appears to me to be probable; for we know that the holy fathers, during sacrifices, observed the solemn rite of tasting the cup; <note n="188"> <div sID="gen102431" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que les saincts peres ont observé ceste ceremonie solennelle de prendre la coupe, et gouster un peu de ce qui estoit dedans</foreign>;” — “that the holy fathers observed this ceremony of taking the cup, and tasting a little of what was within it.”<div eID="gen102431" type="x-p"/> </note> and hence those words of the Psalmist,<div eID="gen102430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102432" type="x-p"/>I will take the cup of salvation,<lb/> and will call on the name of the Lord, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.116.13">Psalm 116:13</reference>.)<div eID="gen102432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102433" type="x-p"/>I have no doubt, therefore, that Christ, according to the ancient custom, tasted <hi type="italic">the cup </hi>in the holy feast, which otherwise could not have been correctly observed; and Luke expressly mentions this, before coming to give an account of the new mystery, which was a totally different institution from the paschal lamb. It was in compliance also with received and ordinary custom, that he is expressly said to have <hi type="italic">given thanks, </hi>after having <hi type="italic">taken the cup. </hi>For at the commencement of the supper, I have no doubt, he prayed, as he was accustomed never to sit down at table without calling on God; but now he wished to discharge once more the same duty, that he might not leave out a ceremony which, I have just now shown, was connected with the sacred act of <hi type="italic">taking the cup </hi>and tasting it. <note n="189"> <div sID="gen102434" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De prende la coupe, et en gouster</foreign>.”<div eID="gen102434" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen102433" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102429" osisID="Luke.22.17" type="section"/>
entries.7079eeecaa059bd3765a8962ad0cecd3985d9d93: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.19" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.19" sID="gen102464" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.19">Luke 22:19</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Which is given for you. </hi>The other two Evangelists leave out this clause, which, however, is far from being superfluous; for the reason why the flesh of Christ becomes <hi type="italic">bread </hi>to us is, that by it salvation was once procured for us. And as the crucified flesh itself is of no advantage but to those who <hi type="italic">eat </hi>it by faith, so, on the other hand, the <hi type="italic">eating </hi>of it would be unmeaning, and of hardly any value, were it not in reference to the sacrifice which was once offered. Whoever then desires that the flesh of Christ should afford nourishment to him, let him look at it as having been offered on the cross, that it might be the price of our reconciliation with God. But what Matthew and Mark leave out in reference to the symbol of <hi type="italic">bread, </hi>they express in reference to the <hi type="italic">cup, </hi>saying, that <hi type="italic">the blood was to be shed for the remission of sins; </hi>and this observation must be extended to both clauses. So then, in order that we may feed aright on the flesh of Christ, we must contemplate the sacrifice of it, because it was necessary that it should have been once given for our salvation, that it might every day be given to us.<div eID="gen102465" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.19" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102464" osisID="Luke.22.19" type="section"/>
entries.6387ee3dc3bc250634dad32209bf55ba1f4b63ac: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.28" sID="gen100960" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100961" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.28">Luke 22:28</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">You are they who have continued with me.</hi> Although Luke appears to relate a different discourse of Christ, and one which was delivered at a different time, yet I have no doubt that it refers to the same time. For it is not a continued discourse of Christ that is here related, but detached sentences, without any regard to the order of time, as we shall shortly afterwards have occasion to state. But he employs more words than Matthew; for he declares that, as the apostles had accompanied him, and had <hi type="italic">remained steadfastly in his temptations,</hi> they would also be partakers of his glory. It is asked, in what sense does he call them <hi type="italic">his temptations? </hi>I think that he means the contests by which God tried him and the apostles in common. And properly did he use the word <hi type="italic">temptations; </hi>for, according to the feeling of human nature, his faith and patience were actually tried.<div eID="gen100961" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100960" osisID="Luke.22.28" type="section"/>
entries.31ccaff1808c40ecc114ed4672b7498e62d15ee3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.29" sID="gen100962" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi> <hi type="italic">And I appoint to you the kingdom.</hi> Here he makes them not only judges, but <hi type="italic">kings; </hi>for he shares with them <hi type="italic">the kingdom </hi>which he received from <hi type="italic">the Father</hi> There is an emphasis in the word <hi type="italic">appoint</hi>, that they may not, by warmth and vehemence of desire, hasten too eagerly to possess <hi type="italic">the kingdom </hi>of which he alone has the lawful right to dispose. By his own example, also, he exhorts them to patience; for, though he was ordained by <hi type="italic">the Father </hi>to be a King, yet he was not immediately raised to his glory, but even <hi type="italic">emptied Himself</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.2.7">Philippians 2:7</reference>,) and by the ignominy of the cross obtained kingly honor. To <hi type="italic">eat and drink at his table</hi> is put metaphorically for being made partakers of the same glory.<div eID="gen100963" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100962" osisID="Luke.22.29" type="section"/>
entries.0c8bbedb377e15735deb12a3f4c544502ce12bfe: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.31" sID="gen102490" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.31">Luke 22:31</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Lo</hi>, <hi type="italic">Satan hath desired. </hi>The other two Evangelists relate more briefly and simply, that our Lord foretold to his disciples their fall. But the words of Luke contain more abundant instruction; for Christ does not speak of the future trouble in the way of narrative, but expressly declares, that they will have a contest with <hi type="italic">Satan, </hi>and, at the same <hi type="italic">time, </hi>promises to them victory. It is a highly useful admonition, whenever we meet with any thing that gives us offense, to have always before our eyes the snares of <hi type="italic">Satan; </hi>as Paul also teaches, that<div eID="gen102491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102492" type="x-p"/>we wrestle not with flesh and blood, but with spiritual armies, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.12">Ephesians 6:12</reference>.)<div eID="gen102492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102493" type="x-p"/>The meaning of the words therefore is: “When, a short time hence, you shall see me oppressed, know that <hi type="italic">Satan </hi>employs these arms to fight against you, and that this is a convenient opportunity for destroying your faith.” I have said that this is a useful doctrine, because it frequently happens that, from want of consideration, we are overcome by disregarding temptations, which we would regard as formidable, if we reflected that they are <hi type="italic">the fiery darts </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.16">Ephesians 6:16</reference>) of a vigorous and powerful enemy. And though he now speaks of that singularly fierce attack, by which the disciples, at one time, received dreadful shocks, so that their faith was well nigh extinguished, yet he manifestly conveys a more extensive doctrine, that <hi type="italic">Satan </hi>continually goes about, roaring for his prey. As he is impelled by such furious madness to destroy us, nothing is more unreasonable than that we should give ourselves up to drowsiness. Before there is apparent necessity for fighting, let us already prepare ourselves; for we know that <hi type="italic">Satan </hi>desires our destruction, and with great skill and assiduity seizes on every method of injuring us. And when we come to the conflict, let us know that all temptations, from whatever quarter they come, were forged in the workshop of that enemy.<div eID="gen102493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102494" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That he may sift you as wheat. </hi>The metaphor of <hi type="italic">sifting </hi>is not in every respect applicable; for we have elsewhere seen that the Gospel is compared to a <hi type="italic">winnowing-fan </hi>or <hi type="italic">sieve, </hi>by which the <hi type="italic">wheat </hi>is purified from the <hi type="italic">chaff</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.12">Matthew 3:12</reference>;) but here it simply means to toss up and down, or to shake with violence, because the apostles were driven about with unusual severity by the death of Christ. This ought to be understood, because there is nothing in which Satan takes less delight than the <hi type="italic">purification </hi>of believers. Yet though it be for a different purpose that he shakes them, it is nevertheless true, that they are driven and tossed about in every direction, just as the <hi type="italic">wheat </hi>is shaken by the <hi type="italic">winnowing-fan. </hi>But we shall shortly afterwards see that a still more disastrous fulfillment of these words was experienced by the disciples. And this is what is meant by the words of our Lord, as related by Matthew and Mark: <hi type="italic">you will all be offended at me. </hi>They mean that the disciples will not only be attacked, but will nearly give way; because the ignominious treatment of Christ will quite overpower their minds. For whereas it was their duty to advance steadily with their Master to the cross, fear kept them back. Their infirmity is thus exhibited to them, that by prayers and groans they may betake themselves to God’s holy protection.<div eID="gen102494" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102490" osisID="Luke.22.31" type="section"/>
entries.f086ba5df3a1dce3b4025ed4a798a67b3c6533f7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.35" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.35" sID="gen102515" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102516" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.35">Luke 22:35</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he said to them. </hi>The whole object of this discourse of Christ is to show, that hitherto he spared his disciples, so as to lay on them no heavier burden than they were able to bear. He reminds them of the indulgence exercised during the past time, that they may now prepare themselves with greater alacrity for severer warfare. For why did he, while they were altogether destitute of skill and training, keep them in the shade and in repose, at a distance from the darts of the enemy, except that, by gradually gathering courage and strength during the interval of leisure, they might be better prepared for fighting? The meaning is: “Hitherto you have had an easy and prosperous condition, because I wished to treat you gently, like children; the full time is now come, when I must employ you in labor, like men.” But the comparison which he makes between the two periods is still more extensive; for if they wanted nothing, when they proceeded to discharge their office without taking with them a stock of provisions, when a state of peace allowed them leisure to provide for their necessities, much more now, in the midst of tumult and excitement, ought they to lay aside anxiety about the present life, and run wherever necessity calls them. And although Christ makes special mention of what he had done in reference to the twelve apostles, he shows likewise, that while we are still beginners and weak in faith, he continues to indulge us till we grow up to be men; and, therefore, that they act improperly who devote their leisure to the pursuit of luxuries, which abate the rigor of their faith. And let us not doubt that Christ has regard to us in the present day, since he does not hurry us into the battle while we are still untrained and inexperienced, but, before sending us to the field, supplies us with arms and courage.<div eID="gen102516" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.35" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102515" osisID="Luke.22.35" type="section"/>
entries.10ea648feb2b4dcd3b1092b3aba3cc670b263ae8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.36" sID="gen102517" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">36.</hi> <hi type="italic">But now let him who hath a purse take it. </hi>In metaphorical language he threatens that they will soon meet with great troubles and fierce attacks; just as when a general, intending to lead the soldiers into the field of battle, calls them to arms, and orders them to lay aside every other care, and think of nothing else than fighting, not even to take any thought about procuring food. For he shows them—as is usually done in cases of extreme danger—that every thing must be sold, even to the <hi type="italic">scrip </hi>and the <hi type="italic">purse, </hi>in order to supply them with arms. And yet he does not call them to an outward conflict, but only, under the comparison of fighting, he warns them of the severe struggles of temptations which they must undergo, and of the fierce attacks which they must sustain in spiritual contests. That they might more willingly throw themselves on the providence of God, he first reminded them, as I have said, that God took care to supply them with what was necessary, even when they carried with them no supplies of food and raiment. Having experienced so large and seasonable supplies from God, they ought not, for the future, to entertain any doubt that he would provide for every one of their necessities.<div eID="gen102518" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102517" osisID="Luke.22.36" type="section"/>
entries.100848efbe54d8d85e0dd961a9002ce425bf2690: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.37" sID="gen102519" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37.</hi> <hi type="italic">That this also which is written must be accomplished in me. </hi>This adverb <hi type="italic">also </hi>is emphatic; for Christ means, that he had not <hi type="italic">yet </hi>discharged every part of his office, till he had been ranked with ungodly and wicked men, as if he had been one of their class. But that their minds might not be too much disturbed by the baseness of such a transaction, he quotes a prediction of Isaiah, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.53.12">53:12</reference>) which, it is certain, cannot be explained but as referring to the Messiah. Now since it is there said that he was to be <hi type="italic">reckoned among transgressors, </hi>such a spectacle, however atrocious, ought not to alarm believers, or to alienate them from Christ, who could not have been their Redeemer in any other way than by taking upon himself the shame and disgrace of a wicked man. For nothing is better adapted to remove grounds of offense, when we are alarmed by any strange occurrence, than to acknowledge that it so pleases God, and that whatever takes place by his appointment is not done rashly, or without a good reason; more especially when that which is made evident by the event itself was anciently predicted. Since, then, the disciples ought to expect a Redeemer such as God had formerly promised, and since Isaiah had expressly declared, that in order that he might deliver us from the guilt of offenses the punishment must be <hi type="italic">laid on him, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.53.5 Bible:Isa.53.6">Isaiah 53:5, 6</reference>,) this ought to be sufficient for abating the horror of the disciples, and for preventing them from entertaining less esteem for Christ.<div eID="gen102520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen102521" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For those things which relate to me have an end. </hi>By these words, immediately added, he means that the prophets spoke nothing in vain. For this Greek phrase, <foreign xml:lang="el">τέλος ἔχει</foreign>, <hi type="italic">have an end; </hi>means that they are accomplished, or put in effect. Now when every thing that the prophets spoke is verified by the event, it ought rather to contribute to strengthen our faith, than to strike us with alarm or anxiety. But while Christ encourages and comforts the disciples by this single argument, that all the predictions <hi type="italic">must be accomplished, </hi>the very procedure of the divine purpose contains within itself no ordinary ground of confidence, which is, that Christ was subjected to the condemnation which we deserved, and <hi type="italic">was reconciled among transgressors, </hi>that we, who are <hi type="italic">transgressors, </hi>and loaded with crimes, might be presented by him to the Father as righteous. For we are reckoned pure and free from sins before God, because the Lamb, who was pure and free from every blemish, was placed in our room, as we shah have occasion to state again under the next chapter.<div eID="gen102521" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102519" osisID="Luke.22.37" type="section"/>

38. Lord, lo, here are two swords. It was truly shameful and stupid ignorance, that the disciples, after having been so often informed about bearing the cross, imagine that they must fight with swords of iron. When they say that they have two swords, it is uncertain whether they mean that they are well prepared against their enemies, or complain that they are ill provided with arms. It is evident, at least, that they were so stupid as not to think of a spiritual enemy. As to the inference which the Doctors of Canon Law draw from these words — that their mitered bishops have a double jurisdiction — it is not only an offensive allegory, but a detestable mockery, by which they ridicule the word of God. And it was necessary that the slaves of Antichrist should fall into such madness, of openly trampling under feet, by sacrilegious contempt, the sacred oracles of God.

entries.d94aa0c3b200c02e86e08c21ca6a038bfe0b39c5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.51" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.22.51" sID="gen102629" type="section"/> <div sID="gen102630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.51">Luke 22:51</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And having touched his ear, he healed him. </hi>By his foolish zeal Peter had brought grievous reproach on his Master and his doctrine; and there can be no doubt, that this was a contrivance by which Satan attempted to involve the Gospel in eternal disgrace, as if Christ had kept company with assassins and seditious persons for revolutionary purposes. This, I think, was the reason why Christ healed the wound which Peter had inflicted. But a fearful and amazing stupidity must have seized his adversaries, who were not at all affected by having seen such a miracle. And yet there is the less reason to wonder that they did not see the power of Christ displayed in the person of another, when, after having themselves been laid prostrate by his voice, they still continued to rage, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.18.6">John 18:6</reference>.) Such is the spirit of giddiness by which Satan maddens the reprobate, when the Lord has given them over to blindness. Above all, in the person himself who was healed, there is a striking instance of ingratitude; for neither did the divine power of Christ subdue him to repentance for his hardness, nor was he overcome by kindness so as to be changed from an enemy into a disciple. For it is a foolish imagination of the monks that he was also <hi type="italic">healed </hi>in his soul, that the work of Christ might not be left incomplete; as if the goodness of God were not every day poured out on those who are unworthy.<div eID="gen102630" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.22.51" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen102629" osisID="Luke.22.51" type="section"/>

But (saith our Saviour) <ns0:hi>I have prayed that thy Faith fail not.</ns0:hi> There is a total and a partial failing of Faith. <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi>'s Faith did fail in part; but the <ns0:hi>Seed of God</ns0:hi> did yet abide in him; his Faith did not wholly fail, so will it be with the Faith of every true Disciple of Christ. In hours of great Temptation and Tryal, their <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> may, as to some de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />grees, fail, but totally it shall not. They may be perverted, but they shall again be converted. As the Apostle saith of the Bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dies of the Saints, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.10, 11. <ns0:hi>And if Christ be in you, the Body is Dead, because of Sin, but the Spirit is Life be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause of Righteousness. But if the Spirit of him that raised up Iesus from the Dead, dwell in you, he that raised up Christ from the Dead shall also quicken your Mortal Bodies by his Spirit that dwelleth in you,</ns0:hi> may also be said of their Souls. They have in them a <ns0:hi>Body of Death,</ns0:hi> and they may in an Hour of great Temptations fail, and their gracious Habits may seem to dye. But if the Spirit of God dwelleth in the Soul, he will again quicken their Souls by his Spirit which dwelleth in them. <ns0:hi>And when thou art Converted strengthen thy Brethren.</ns0:hi> That is, when God hath recovered thee from thy fall, and made thee to see thy Error, make an improvment of thy recovery out of the snare of the Devil, by admonishing others to take heed of too much confidence in themselves, and incouraging them not to despair, tho they also may fall into <ns0:hi>Temptation</ns0:hi>; but that the Grace of God shall be sufficient for them.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 And he said unto him, Lord, I am ready to go with thee both into prison, and to death.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 And he said, I tell thee, Peter, the cock shall not crow this day, before that thou shalt thrice de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny that thou knowest me.<ns0:note place="bottom">This is more largely recorded by <ns0:hi>Matth. Ch.</ns0:hi> 26.33, 34, 35. and by <ns0:hi>Mark, Ch.</ns0:hi> 14.27, 28, 29, 30. See the Notes on those places.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 And he said unto them, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 10.9.</ns0:note> When I sent you with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye any thing? And they said, Nothing.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 Then said he unto them, But now he that hath a purse, let him take <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> and likewise <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> scrip: and he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:323" />37 For I say unto you, that this that is written, must yet be accomplished in me, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mark 15.28.</ns0:note> And he was rec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />koned among the transgressours: For the things con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning me have an end.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 And they said, Lord, behold, here <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> two swords. And he said unto them, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>t is enough.<ns0:note place="bottom">Those who interpret, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 35, 36. as a Precept of our Saviours imposing a Duty upon his Disciples: or a <ns0:hi>Counsel</ns0:hi> concerning the providing Arms which they might use for the protection and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fence of themselves, will not only find a difficulty to reconcile their notion of it, to several other precepts, and the Will of God declared by the Apostles practice, who never went about by force, and Arms to defend themselves in the first Plantation and Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pagation of the Gospel: but also to Reconcile it to the last Words of our Saviour, who said, when his Disciples told him they had <ns0:hi>two Swords, It is enough.</ns0:hi> Which he would never have said, if he had intended any such thing; for <ns0:hi>two Swords</ns0:hi> was much too little to have Conquered that Multitude of Adversa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries, which the Disciples of Christ were to meet with. Our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour doth doubtless speak in a Figure, and all that he intendeth amounteth but to this. Hitherto I have been with you, and you have had my special protection; tho you went out without a Purse, or a Scrip; yet you have wanted nothing; tho you went without a Sword, yet none did you any harm. But the time is now come, when the posture of your Affairs will be much al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ered; your Friends will be few, your Enemies many, therefore you stand concerned to make as good <ns0:hi>Preparation</ns0:hi> as you can do in those things, that are consistent with the general precepts that I have given you. The Tragedy will begin with me; for what is written of him must now be accomplished, <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 53.12. <ns0:hi>He was numbred amongst the Transgressors</ns0:hi>; I must be brought before Magistrates as a common Malefactor, and han<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged on a Cross betwixt two Thieves. <ns0:hi>And the things concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing me shall shortly have an end</ns0:hi>: you will next come upon the Stage, and therefore prepare what in you lyeth for the perfor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mance of your part.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 26.36. Mark 14.32.</ns0:note> And he came out, and went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives; and his disciples also followed him.<ns0:note place="bottom">Both <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> say, he went to a place called <ns0:hi>Geth<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />semane,</ns0:hi> but that makes no difference, for whether <ns0:hi>Gethsemane</ns0:hi> signifyeth a Village, or a Garden, or a Valley, all agree it was at the Foot of the Mount of <ns0:hi>Olives.</ns0:hi> It was a place to which our Saviour had used to go ever since he came to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and lay in his way to <ns0:hi>Bethany.</ns0:hi> He went thither to pray, and his Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples followed him,</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 And when he was at the place, he said unto them, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 26.41.</ns0:note> Pray, that ye enter not into tempta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion.<ns0:note place="bottom">When he came to the <ns0:hi>Mount</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Olives,</ns0:hi> he first setteth his Disciples to that Work, which at this Day was proper for them. <ns0:hi>Pray, that ye enter not into Temptation,</ns0:hi> that if it be the Will of God, you may be delivered from such an Hour of Try<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al as I am entring into; or at least that you may not be over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />come by it. That my <ns0:hi>Tryals</ns0:hi> which you will presently <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Witnesses unto, and your own which you shall hereafter meet with, may have no Power upon you to withdraw you from your Work in the Publication, or Profession of my Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel. The other two Evangelists make mention of our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our's taking <ns0:hi>Peter,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iames,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> with him, yet more privately. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> mentioneth not that but goeth on.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 26.39.</ns0:note> And he was withdrawn from them about a stones cast, and kneeled down and prayed.<ns0:note place="bottom">Whether from the Eight, or from <ns0:hi>Peter, Iames</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> also the Evangelist doth not tell us; but some are of opinion, that he took the three Disciples along, to joyn with him in Prayer, from whom some account might be given of the sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stance of his Prayer, which followeth. I rather think he was alone.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note> willing, remove this cup from me:<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">John 6.38.</ns0:note> nevertheless not my will, but thine be done.<ns0:note place="bottom">We have a larger account given us of our Saviour's Prayer, both by <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark, Matth.</ns0:hi> 26. from 39. to 46. and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14. from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 35. to 42. Heb. 5.7.</ns0:note> And being in an agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.<ns0:note place="bottom">We have formerly opened these Verses in our Notes, on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 44, 45, 46. where we took them in, as being a part of the History of our Saviour's praying before his passion.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="46">46 And said unto them, Why <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>t ye enter into temptation.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Relations which <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> give us, are both more particular, than that given us by <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> to which we refer the <ns0:hi>Reader. Luke</ns0:hi> speaketh but of his praying once. <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith he prayed thrice. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> mentioneth nothing of his withdrawing with <ns0:hi>Peter, Iames</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> from the o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Eight, <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> both mention it. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> mak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth mention of an <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi> appearing to him; of the <ns0:hi>Agony</ns0:hi> in which he was, and his <ns0:hi>Sweating drops as it were of Blood,</ns0:hi> which neither <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> nor <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> take notice of, yet we must not think, that either any one of the <ns0:hi>Evangelists,</ns0:hi> or all of them together give a perfect account of all the Words our Saviour used in these Prayers, only they tell us the Sum of them in different Words: but see the Annotations on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 46.39. and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14. where we have fully considered whatsoever is said by any of the Evangelists upon this Argument.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 And while he yet spake, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">John 18.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> behold, a multitude, and he that was called Judas, one of the twelve, went before them, and drew near unto Jesus, to kiss him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 But Jesus said unto him, Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.47, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14.43.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">49 When they which were about him, saw what would follow, they said unto him, Lord, shall we smite with the sword?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="50">50 And one of them <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mark 14.47 John 18.10, 11</ns0:note> smote the servant of the high priests, and cut off his right ear.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="51">51 And Jesus answered and said, Suffer ye thus far. And he touched his ear, and healed him.<ns0:note place="bottom">No other Evangelist but <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> hath this passages perfect. What he hath we have opened in our Notes, on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.41.52. because it tendeth to compleat that part of the Histo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry there discoursed, concerning Christs being apprehended. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> relates it with more Circumstances, telling us that it was <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> who drew the Sword, and that his Name whose Ear was cut off, was <ns0:hi>Malchus,</ns0:hi> and relateth some further Words used by our Saviour to <ns0:hi>Peter,</ns0:hi> which we shall further consider in their places. This rash act of <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> might have cost him dear, for it made a Kinsman of <ns0:hi>Malchus</ns0:hi> take such notice of him, as he was very near being accused by him, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 18.26. Swords are dangerous things for us to use, until God puts them into our Hands. <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> ought not only to have asked his Master if he should smite with the Sword<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but also to have staid his Hand till Christ had given him an Answer.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="53">53 When I was daily with you in the temple, ye stretched forth no hands against me: but this is your hour, and the power of darkness.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.55. and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14.48, 49.                <ns0:p n="71">71 And they said, What need we any further witness? for we our selves have heard of his own mouth.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our blessed Lord before his Death passed two Trials or Exami<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nations. The one before the Jewish <ns0:hi>Sanhedrim,</ns0:hi> whose proper Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vince it was to try such as were accused, as <ns0:hi>false Prophets,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Blasphemers.</ns0:hi> This was a kind of <ns0:hi>Ecclesiastical Court.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>High Priest</ns0:hi> was the chief <ns0:hi>Iudge</ns0:hi> in it, and we are told that they used to sit in his Palace.
